claims.text: Tribological performance improves as ambient temperature rises from room temperature toward approximately 300°C.
The improvement below approximately 300°C is caused by enhanced formation of a tribochemical oxide layer that acts as a solid lubricant.
Tribological performance degrades significantly at or beyond a critical boundary of approximately 300°C.
High-temperature degradation is caused by accelerated oxidation, matrix softening, and loss of coating adhesion.
The initial material is a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory HEA coating deposited on a 304 stainless-steel substrate.
Annealing gives the coating high hardness and improved adhesion.
The proposed intervention tests the coating from room temperature through 600°C against a steel counterball.
Sliding occurs in air under constant load and sliding velocity.
Temperature-dependent tribochemical layers contain oxides such as CuO, Fe2O3, and Cr2O3.
Temperature changes dislocation mobility and diffusion rates within the HEA lattice.
Below 300°C, the HEA maintains high hardness and develops a thin protective oxide layer that reduces friction and wear.
At 300°C, tribochemical reactions and oxide formation are associated with a high coefficient of friction.
Above 300°C, accelerated diffusion and oxidation produce thick, brittle oxide scales and soften the HEA matrix.
Tribological behavior is governed by competition between beneficial oxide lubrication and detrimental thermal softening and oxidation.
Wear rate increases nonlinearly with temperature and shows a sharp increase above approximately 300°C, accompanied by COF greater than 1.0 and wear rate greater than 10^-5 mm^3/N m.
The annealed coating exhibits steady-state, low abrasive wear at room temperature and moderate temperature.
At higher temperatures, the wear mode transitions to severe adhesive and oxidative wear.
At room temperature, the annealed coating has a COF of approximately 0.25 and a wear rate of approximately 6.4×10^-6 mm^3/N m.
Beyond approximately 300°C, COF exceeds 1.0 and wear rate exceeds 2.5×10^-5 mm^3/N m.
The transition temperature varies with HEA composition, coating microstructure, humidity, and oxygen partial pressure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says performance initially improves as temperature rises up to about 300°C, but the stated values show deterioration from RT to 300°C: COF rises from about 0.25 to 1.5 and wear rate rises from 6.4×10^-6 to 2.5×10^-5 mm^3/N m.
The hypothesis characterizes oxide formation up to the threshold as lubricating, whereas the mechanism also associates oxide-forming tribochemical reactions at 300°C with high friction.
